rows.record: Chaetoceros is the most species-rich diatom genus in Hudson Bay microscope surveys; C. compressus and C. septentrionalis were the most common, "particularly in waters adjacent to the Churchill and Nelson rivers"; dominant diatoms with Thalassiosira in Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay by 18S.

Nitzschia longissima is in the most common, widespread group (53–90 of 130 samples, 1975); Nitzschia and Navicula (led by N. frigida) dominate the April–May ice-algal bloom in southeastern Hudson Bay.

Thalassiosira gravida and T. nordenskioeldii are common and widespread; Thalassiosira prominent in open northwestern Hudson Bay. Minidiscus itself is not reported (small cells are easily missed by microscopy).
Micromonas polaris and Bathycoccus prasinos dominated the ice-edge picophytoplankton in June 2018 and increased toward ice-covered stations ("pico-phytoplankton-based food web under the ice").
Diaphanoeca undulata and Calliacantha spp. were the named choanoflagellates in Hudson Bay, most abundant in open water.
Golden-brown algae are common in river-influenced southern Hudson Bay surface waters; chrysophytes (Ochromonas) co-dominate Arctic sea ice in 18S surveys.
Calanus glacialis and C. hyperboreus are the dominant Arctic copepods in Hudson Bay; C. glacialis overwinters near Churchill and feeds under the ice on ice algae.
Ciliates reported as exceptionally abundant (Belcher Islands, August), grazing the diatom bloom; not resolved below phylum.
A classic Arctic ice-attached diatom, but not named in the Hudson Bay sources checked (may be counted with Chaetoceros by microscopy).
Fragilaria-type diatoms are listed only as freshwater taxa; a Churchill River plume origin is possible.
Not resolved in the sources; radiolarians increase at deeper central Hudson Bay stations.
Not reported from Hudson Bay; Picochlorum is mostly warm/brackish. Median protein identity 86% suggests an Arctic relative, not Picochlorum itself.

Laminaria, Agarum, Alaria and Fucus occur in Hudson Bay (washed up on beaches; kelp nitrate uptake inshore at Saqvaqjuac), so kelp material in intake water is plausible; but EE01 is 0% BUSCO and 1.5% coding, not a genome.

Dinoflagellates (Heterocapsa, Gymnodiniales, Gyrodinium) dominate summer surface waters and Phaeocystis pouchetii is widespread, but neither produced a MAG: dinoflagellate genomes are huge and repetitive, and CMO sampling was winter–spring.
